utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Trbojevic into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I address the Defence on the following issues, as far as protective measures are concerned in view of -- no, not protective measures. On 92 bis admission KRAJ 431 in relation to Sokolac, in the statement, the witness talks about a book, a book that we are informed was disclosed to the Defence early March and a 30-page English summary and since the Defence reserved the right to make any further submissions in relation to the admission on the basis of the information in that book, we wonder whether there are any further submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I wonder as well, Your Honour, and I shall locate the book and see what the point is. At the moment, I'm quite unable to give Your Honour any information at all in relation to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could also pay attention to KRAJ 674 in relation to Zvornik where on the 2nd of March, two statements were disclosed which might give rise to further submissions as well so that we have the final position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, I will attend to those and put them on to my to-do list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will hope they are soon on your done list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have both lists, one of them, of course, is permanent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, first of all, welcome again. Thank you for coming back. It's quite an effort, the Chamber is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony last week, you have given a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. You are still bound by that solemn declaration. I also informed you at that time that if there's any answer which you would -- if there is any question which you think answering might incriminate yourself, then you can then address the Court and we'll see whether we will compel you to answer that question or whether we leave it and allow you not to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your interview with the -- Mr. Margetts, it mainly was, you talked about Mr. Maksimovic and you said that he was influential as "leader of the caucus," was the way it was put, that's as the leader of the SDS members caucus in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, could we have a page reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 18 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've got two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the first one, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the March one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber how you would rate and assess the level of influence that Mr. Maksimovic had?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic was the president of the deputies' club at the Assembly. He led this club. What exactly his position in the party was, I'm not sure I knew and I couldn't tell you now. I knew that he came from Foca, and in that area around Foca he enjoyed some authority in the party. What exactly his position was within the party, I can't tell you exactly. I believe he was also president of that Serbian cultural society called Prosveta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, the question was not what his position in the party was, the question was how you would rate and assess the level of influence which might be not directly related to positions he held. If you don't know, no problem, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not tell you anything specific about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on then to another point. At page 30, it is, Your Honour, of the same interview, -- Your Honour, I don't believe it's unfair, I'm not troubling the witness with the B/C/S copy, these are short reference points in the interviews at this stage. It was put to you by Mr. Margetts, he said, "So operationally, you think the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Ministry of Defence, and to some extent, Ministry of Justice was being run by Karadzic and Krajisnik," and I believe it's fair to comment that the word "operationally" was introduced by Mr. Margetts and was not picking up a specific word of yours. But in answer to that, you said, "Yes, the police and the army definitely, and when justice is concerned, Karadzic was in capacity of his authority. The function he had was making decision of appointment so practically the justice was also in his hands." Now, I want to break those three down separately, the police, the army, and the justice. Mr. Trbojevic, do you, in fact, have any knowledge yourself of Mr. Krajisnik being involved operationally in the running of the police.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge yourself of Mr. Krajisnik being involved operationally in the activities and running of the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question then, to you Mr. Trbojevic is why did you say then that when Mr. Margetts put it to you that operationally the Ministry of Internal Affairs, of Defence, and to some extent the Ministry of Justice was being run by Karadzic and Krajisnik, you answered that with a "yes." What was the basis on which you gave that answer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I have already explained this in some detail using the example of the Ministry of Justice. As for the Ministry of Defence, that is the minister of defence and the minister of the police who were reporting to the president of the republic, I believe I also said more than once that this link bypassed the Prime Minister. Mr. Margetts was trying to formulate questions in the way that was most convenient to him and I had no reason to jump at his every word and challenge things. My job was to tell what I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. So your "yes" was based on circumventing the Prime Minister in reporting; is that what you intended to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I intended to say that the link between the minister of defence and the minister of police with the president was stronger and it bypassed the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question put to you by Mr. Margetts was about Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. You explained that as far as the Ministry of Justice was concerned, it was your -- you were focussing on Karadzic, would that be different for the other ministries, that's police and army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Formally speaking, the minister of police and the minister of Defence report to the president of the republic as to the Supreme Commander in a state of war. However, the fact that Karadzic and Krajisnik sit in the same building and see each other and cooperate every day remains. We, from outside, never witnessed the situation in which one of them would have some information while the other one wouldn't have it. In practical terms, whatever was reported to one of them should have come or reached the desk of the other as well. That was the practical implication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "should have reached," at the same time I hear you saying that it could not have been otherwise. Is that -- that's more or less an assumption. Is that what you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I did not sit together with them, I can only assume that it was so. But that assumption is based on the fact that they were sitting next to each other and from their conduct, one could never conclude that one of them had more information than the other or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your proposition that you never witnessed the situation in which one of the two of them would have some information while the other wouldn't have it, Mr. Trbojevic, the practical position must have been that you were generally not in a position to test that, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had neither occasion to test it nor any need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were the judge, weren't you, in the -- in a --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- case brought against -- it was a criminal case, wasn't it, brought against Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you expressed, and I just invite you to confirm what you say. In your second interview in May of this year, and it would be at page 12 of the English in the middle of the page there's an answer that begins, -- well there's a question from Mr. Margetts, "It's okay. Do you recall the decision? Do you recall that case clearly and what, in fact, occurred?" I hope Your Honours are able to -- to find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It should be on or very near to page 12, Your Honour. It should be on page 12 of the second interview transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know there's been some -- may have been some discrepancies. I have it at page 13 if that's of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is of great assistance, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've all suffered, Your Honour, a bit, from the different versions of these interviews and slight discrepancies in numbering. The passage I have, anyway, I hope Your Honours now have it, it's -- yes. Mr. Trbojevic says, "I remember a lot. I remember rather well."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And first point was, you said, "I was convinced there was no evidence." And then about four lines from the bottom of that answer, you are recorded in the English as having said, "It looked, it seemed like it was something framed by the police." And then about 20 or 30 lines further on which may or may not be over a page, about three quarters of the way through a long answer from you, there's a reference to "Then we had like construction expert and then we established that that bill was exact. It had on this bill exactly what was done as work," and that was a bill which, from a private constructor, that Mr. Krajisnik had paid. And then the end of the answer you said, "And it was more than obvious that he was like ... that was a witness ... police he was like a police witness who was like, forgiven sequence of many activities in order to testify against Krajisnik and Karadzic. On the other, on the other side, there was no material evidence on who/which would support his testimony." I just invite you to confirm, Mr. Trbojevic, that that is your view, those were your conclusions and that remains your assessment of that case brought against Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, I stated exactly what was done in that case, what I decided in that case. It's all written in the judgement. I believe that it is also stated that the Supreme Court reversed the judgement and ordered a retrial; however, my colleague, the new judge, made the same decision as I did. The Prosecutor filed an appeal, I believe it was Nurija Hodzic, the republican prosecutor, gave up on that appeal, so the decision of the court became valid, came into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the ultimate result was a complete acquittal for Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From your knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik and his work, if somebody was, in relation to political activities, police activities, army activities, any of these things that were going on at that time in the summer of 1992, if anybody was reporting to Mr. Krajisnik, would you expect to see written instructions, orders, memoranda, and reports from Mr. Krajisnik relating to those matters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them and I have no knowledge about him issuing any orders, written instructions, or such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. My question was a slightly different one, Mr. Trbojevic. It was asking you, based on your knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik, in that situation, would you expect if Mr. Krajisnik was being reported to, to see such material coming from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't see any such thing although I understand the logic behind your question. My conclusion would be that it would -- that one could expect that Mr. Krajisnik serious person whether or not takes everything very seriously, should respond to people with instructions, a comment, an order, or something like that. But having seen none of that, I can't say that it happened. That it was exactly that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put it a different way, Mr. Trbojevic. Mr. Krajisnik is a very well-organised man in his work, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And part of his approach to organisation is that he does very often log things, note things, make lists in writing; do you know enough about his work to be able to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say I know enough because I was not a member of his office, but I could see easily that he was always writing something down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were asked, and this is at page -- I'm going to have to do my best on these page references, Your Honour. It should be at page 44 -- 43 or 44 of the English transcript of the second interview. You were asked by Mr. Margetts, or in a sense you were not asked by Mr. Margetts, he said, "I am" -- Mr. Margetts says, "I am not interested in peace negotiations or peace plans."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope Your Honours have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 45 in our version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He sags "I'm not interested in peace negotiations or peace plans." And you said, "But negotiations, talks about the peace plans was the -- was the basis of the politics." Then Mr. Margetts said, "I'm not interested in them because they are on the public record and I know everything about them. There's nothing ..." And then you said, "But you don't know what we were talking about." Mr. Margetts said, "No, there's nothing you can tell me that is of any interest to me because I am very well informed on that peace negotiations ..." And then he, well, steered you, I think perhaps that's a fair way of putting it, steered you on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that continues, I think it would be more fair to characterise the latter portion of Mr. Margetts's remarks as explaining the reason why he was asking the witness not to go into Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. detail about peace negotiations and that was a limited time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, fair or not. I mean, Mr. Margetts is not at trial here. I establish that at that moment, Mr. Margetts was not interested to hear any further from the witness for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it that Mr. Stewart was not blaming Mr. Margetts but was just representing what was in the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's touching that Mr. Tieger should leap to Mr. Margetts's defence, but I was just intending to be just descriptive; I hope I was. The -- but what I was going to ask you, Mr. Trbojevic, was to please expand upon the answer which was not pursued. Then when you said, "Negotiations, talks about the peace plans was the basis of the politics." And please explain to the Trial Chamber what you meant and what you mean by that,"... those negotiations and talks were the basis of the politics."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say quite simply that it was a fact of life that the activity of the National Assembly concentrated, for the most part, on those ongoing negotiations. Every time that a group of our representatives at those negotiations would come to the Assembly, meetings were held where we discussed everything that was tabled at the negotiations, what was noted, what the International Community offered or demanded, what we can accept, what we can't accept, in which way. So most of our time, and most of our energy had to be devoted to deliberations of this peace process, the prospects and the possible consequences of their failure, what sanctions we could expect in the event of failure. You will probably remember that the contact group decided at one point to interrupt these negotiations and suspended all contact with representatives of the Serbian side and so on and so forth. It was simply the central topic, the centre of attention. Everything revolved around it. Everything depended on it. So we were busy considering whether the war was coming to an end, whether we could expect an end, whether we could expect international sanctions. It was the main practical issue, the central issue of the entire life of our Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, do you remember the adoption of the law on supplementing the constitutional law for implementing the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That's a bit of a mouthful, but early in June 1992, the Presidency adopted that law, to try and refresh your memory, which related to the expansion of the Presidency during a state of war. Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I have any concrete recollections of the actual conversation. The date was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you recall that provision was made for the Presidency to be expanded during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made quite a few comments about that later on. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is correct, as far as you're concerned, is it, Mr. Trbojevic, that no -- there was, in fact, no declaration of a state of war made by the Bosnian Serb leadership, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, at the beginning of 1992, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in fact, by the Bosnian Serb leadership or organs at any time in 1992, or at no time was there a declaration of a state of war; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, "you don't think so," did you say? Did I read and hear that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. That may be one of those ambiguous answers, Your Honour. Are you saying that you can't be sure but you think there was not such a declaration of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the dates when -- who declared war on who. That's what I meant. As far as I can remember, in 1992, the Serb side did not declare a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it your view, as a lawyer at the time that -- well, did you have a view on whether the expanded Presidency was legally constituted or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view was that first and foremost, a state of war should not be declared. I thought that moving on to a regimen of a state of war would require legal regulations and institutions that would lend themselves to organising a state of war throughout society. And since I knew that we did not have the legal regulations or institutions required, and we had a government that was more or less organised along civil lines, we did not manage to have a kind of organisation which would be normal, let alone move on to wartime authorities. My position was that that should not be done. In principle, it is difficult to justify an organ like the War Presidency which includes members of the Presidency, the president of the Assembly, as the representative of the legislature, and the Prime Minister as the representative of the executive government. This is an adding up of different functions that is hard to justify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Why do you say that it's hard to justify, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal system, the division of powers, the democratic independence between the different branches of government is thereby destroyed completely. There is no parliamentary life in that way. There is no control over legality or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were asked about exercise of executive powers. This was at page 81 of the -- I'm sorry, it was at page 33. I think it should be page 33 of the transcript of your second interview, the one in May. I hope Your Honours have -- as a reference point, a question from Mr. Margetts, "Your observations at the time was that Krajisnik was more organised and an effective decision maker." If Your Honours have that as a reference point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet, but we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It should be either page 33 or very close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then I -- that's a reference point because I'm then skipping to Mr. Margetts's next question where he says, "Did you observe that it was Krajisnik that was exercising executive decision-making power?" That was his question to you, Mr. Trbojevic. And then you said, "There were no really executive decisions that we could see, but you could see them at some meetings ..." Just pausing there, when you say "there were no really executive decisions that we could see," who, in that answer, is "we"? Or are "we"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that I meant the government as an organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Then moving on in your answer, then, you said, "No really executive decisions that we could see." Then you went on to say, "But you could see them at some meetings at the Assembly, and then at the Krajisnik's cabinet at the Assembly before leaving Sarajevo and also at the club of deputies." I'm not going to ask you about the Assembly, Mr. Trbojevic, because it's a public meeting of which there's a record, but the next point, "Then at Krajisnik's cabinet at the Assembly." Are you -- you're talking about -- when you say "Krajisnik's cabinet," meetings that you personally attended, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I do not quite understand what you just read out to me. As for meetings in Mr. Krajisnik's office when he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest then perhaps Mr. Trbojevic should have the B/C/S transcript - this should be found at page 28 - if he's not readily grasping the point. I'm very much obliged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope there's only one version of that. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you find it, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can pick it up, I think we've even got lines for you. You should be able to pick that up around line 29/30, you should pick up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two versions because mine does not contain any lines, the one I just gave to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, a lined version of B/C/S was produced at some point but perhaps that luxurious item has got mislaid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, do you find the line where it reads, "Did you observe that it was Krajisnik that was exercising executive decision making power?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it's your next answer or your answer to that question, Mr. Trbojevic, that I'm concentrating on. "There were no really executive decisions that we could see," and you had indicated a few minutes ago that you believed that by "we" you must have meant the government. Then you go on to say, "But you could see them at some meetings at the Assembly," and I said I wouldn't ask you now about the Assembly, "And then at Krajisnik's cabinet at the Assembly before leaving Sarajevo." So I was asking you then with reference to "Krajisnik's cabinet at the Assembly before leaving Sarajevo," whether you're talking there about meetings that you personally attended? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you give, then, an example of an executive -- what you would describe as an executive decision taken at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said already that I haven't seen any executive decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to clarify then, Mr. Trbojevic, your first couple of lines of that answer you gave in the interview reads, "There were no really executive decisions that we could see, but you could see them at some meetings." So Mr. Trbojevic, I'm just suggesting as an introduction to this question, the way it reads is that there's some qualification of that assertion that you could see them sometimes. But is it this, Mr. Trbojevic, you're essentially saying that whether or not there were some minor or insignificant decisions taken, the first line of that answer is your position: There were no really executive decisions that you could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't going to seek the full response as long as the focus was sort of on locations, but if it's a matter of interpreting what the witness meant by the first part of his answer, I think his attention needs to be drawn to the full answer especially given the potential ambiguities of what is meant by "them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I certainly wasn't intending -- well, two things. I thought for a moment to invite the witness to read the answer but I rather assume that a very experienced lawyer by Mr. Trbojevic would have cast his eyes down those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you, in fact, while we've been considering this, Mr. Trbojevic, have you had an opportunity to read the whole of the eight lines of your answer there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could invite the witness to further clarify what he exactly meant. Mr. Trbojevic, could you further elaborate on what you -- what your answer was about? Because there seems to start with executive decisions which you say and you repeated it now, you have not seen, and then you continue with matters that happened at meetings of which you at least said that the meetings and the -- Mr. Krajisnik's cabinet at the Assembly, you attended. Could you explain exactly what you meant by this answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, the investigator and I were not discussing decisions here but rather the relationship between Karadzic and Krajisnik. I was explaining that I had the opportunity at Mr. Krajisnik's office before leaving Sarajevo, and after that, at the MP's club, on several occasions of seeing debates, discussions taking place, different views being expounded. I described here that Krajisnik always made a maximum effort and that he managed to do so to treat Karadzic as his boss. And I presented my own assessment that when there was a discussion regarding particular issues, that Krajisnik's word carried more weight in terms of quality, in terms of content, than Karadzic's. I presented that as my own assessment of the many discussions that were not an introduction to decisions that were to be made but simply debates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Karadzic present during those discussions as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I -- when I read this, it was not entirely clear to me whether in those discussions on certain issues, it was Mr. Krajisnik who convinced the others that the line of the boss, Karadzic, was the one to be followed, or whether I have to read it that you say that when Krajisnik and Karadzic were both present and discussions on those issues developed, that finally, the views of Mr. Krajisnik at the end were the prevailing ones. Is it the first interpretation or the second or neither of them which is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The latter is the case. Krajisnik's viewpoint would prevail more often but that is my assessment of the talks from before the war, before the Constitution was passed on the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then countless meetings of the deputies' club, many talks related to the peace negotiations, and so on and so forth. Quite simply, I think that it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A noticeable difference between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik was this, wasn't it, that whereas Dr. Karadzic had, as you have confirmed before, a tendency to shoot from the hip, Mr. Krajisnik did not; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I never heard that figure of speech before, this shoot from the hip, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I only go on the fact that I believe I used it very specifically in this -- in the course of your evidence and it appeared to be translated without difficulty. But perhaps I'm wrong about that. Mr. -- I'll do it again then, Mr. Trbojevic. Dr. Karadzic had a tendency to fire off rather extreme statements and assertions and arguments, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "extreme," but rapid, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll put a slightly different question then. Dr. Karadzic had a tendency, perhaps rapidly, to produce statements or arguments which appeared not to be fully thought out by him.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was prone to that, to -- not to go into a more profound analysis, but to formulate what he wanted to say more superficially, though rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. I beg your pardon, I thought you were going to go into a more profound analysis there which I was in the interests of time going to discourage?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik did not have that tendency, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that in a group meeting, or any other sort, but in the meeting of a nature that you described, Mr. Krajisnik's views would be regarded Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. consistently more respectfully because he produced measured, more cautiously-expressed views; is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What were -- first of all, when you talk about "the Krajisnik cabinet" you're talking about -- you said Dr. Karadzic was there, you describe it as Mr. Krajisnik's cabinet, so what -- Mr. Krajisnik was in the chair then, was he, at those meetings at the Assembly before leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there purpose to plan and discuss what was going to happen or might happen at forthcoming Assembly sessions? Was that one of the elements of the discussion at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think you've already made it clear that those meetings included, but just so there's no ambiguity, those meetings included discussions about peace negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in addition to that, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Trbojevic, could you give us an example on where the views of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic were not the same and where Mr. Krajisnik's views would prevail at the end of the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a concrete example. What I described here were several meetings of different types and of different substance. Meetings at Mr. Krajisnik's office while he was president of the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, those were different discussions in terms of what is expected at the next meeting, what can be -- of the Assembly, what can be expected from the SDA MPs, what can be expected from the HDZ MPs. If you remember, especially regarding the subject whether Bosnia-Herzegovina is going to seek independence and separation from Yugoslavia, things like that. How the club of deputies of the SDS would respond to that. How they would react to that. Because we were not interested in having Bosnia-Herzegovina separate from the -- from Yugoslavia. So we were in agreement about 90 per cent, all of us. There was no confrontation. I'm just describing the situation there in terms of my own assessment. Krajisnik was more rational, more serious, more profound in dealing with problems and simply what he would say would carry more weight than what Karadzic would say. That situation would repeat itself when we discussed the peace talks during the war, that situation again repeated itself when we discussed our relations with Serbia which later on imposed a blockade against us. That is what I meant. I cannot give a concrete example now in terms of Krajisnik as for that and Krajisnik as for that, I do not have that kind of confrontational example, a clear example of that kind in terms of the things that I have been telling you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then try to find out whether I understood you well. Are you saying that when you discussed issues as what position to take in the Assembly by the SDS or what position to present during peace negotiations, that if there were differences of view, that often, Mr. Krajisnik's view would prevail; that is to say, that his views were then adopted by SDS members that took such a position then in the Assembly or that negotiators would adopt such a position to take in the negotiations. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking of the Assembly, yes, it is a correct understanding. As for outside negotiations, Karadzic was more strong headed, I would say. He was less amenable to specific suggestions and proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this phenomena was there as far as the Assembly is concerned but as far as international negotiations were concerned, Mr. Krajisnik's views would not, in a similar way, be adopted by those who would present those positions at the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said, speaking of international negotiations, Karadzic was more likely to hold on firmly to his position and generally speaking, as time went on, he was less and less amenable to reason, less amenable to the suggestions of others. You could influence him less and less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you made, although you first put on one line, you now make a clear distinction between issues to be discussed at peace negotiations rather than in Assembly meetings. If you say Karadzic was less amenable to follow the views and he would go his own way, what could you tell us about others being present at those meetings? Would Karadzic go against the majority view or would Karadzic convince the others present that his view, which he finally then would take, was better than another view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Outside the deliberations that were held within the club of deputies or within the Assembly, I did not attend the talks they had with others. My impression was that whatever Mrs. Plavsic said, Mr. Koljevic, and Mr. Buha, did not mean anything to Mr. Karadzic. How he treated Mr. Krajisnik's views in those internal meetings, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed. Yes, Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the relations between these two men, Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, that you had the opportunity to witness, did you see Mr. Krajisnik disapprove of anything that Mr. Karadzic had said in the presence of other people and in your presence, namely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could not see anything of the kind in public. Mr. Krajisnik was consistent in his deference to Karadzic as the leader and he would never allow himself to openly and clearly distance himself from Mr. Karadzic, his views, in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you expect from him that type of reaction? Did you regret that he did not react in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes I did. But I did not really expect him to confront Karadzic because ever since I've known them, I've never seen a direct confrontation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then in what circumstances did you regret that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many rounds of talks starting with the preparation and the declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina through its Constitution and other steps. There were many times when we felt we were on the threshold of a peace agreement up to the moment when we were facing a real possibility of international sanctions just as Serbia did. I am at a loss for a specific example though. I really can can't think of anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question in this respect. You, in your answer about whether Mr. Krajisnik, in meetings -- the question was whether you saw Mr. Krajisnik disapprove of anything that Mr. Karadzic had said in the presence of other people, and in your presence, namely. Now, you focused your answer on what Mr. Krajisnik did in public but the question also included situations where just you or perhaps a few others were present which were not public meetings. What happened in those meetings? Did you there ever witness Mr. Krajisnik disapproving with what Mr. Karadzic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were very few meetings attended by a small number of people that I attended, so I do not have such an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say there were small meetings and thus which of course is not conclusive. If you were talking about smaller meetings, I mean any meeting that was not for the public eye, whether there were 5 people or 10 people or 20 people, that's not what I'm interested in. Just non-public meetings irrespective of the number of people present, whether at such occasions you ever witnessed Mr. Krajisnik to disapprove of what Mr. Karadzic said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At such smaller meetings, I attended only a couple of times. I can't tell you that I attended many of them when I didn't. Whether it was the constitutional committee or some ad hoc group, I can't remember now but I can't think of any example where they would be in open confrontation. With Mr. Krajisnik, you could see that he was making an effort to avoid confrontation and to preserve peace within the house, so to speak, especially in the Assembly, and it was something that you could clearly see in him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not talking about the Assembly because these were, as far as I understand, public meetings. But in your earlier answers, you said about Mr. Krajisnik's views prevailing at the end. Doesn't that require that there were at least two views that were not concurring completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to explain this to you. When I mentioned the effort to obstruct the demand of Bosnia and Herzegovina to separate from Yugoslavia, I said that there was no disagreement regarding the basic principle and the basic commitment among us. All the talk was about the practical steps that could be made in one way or another. Later, when peace negotiations started, since there were many rounds of these negotiations, concentrating on various aspects and various options that, for us, meant different kinds of obligations, different maps with varying amounts of territory supposed to remain within the republic, varying amounts of territory lost to other parties, internal discussions were necessary; however, I can't say the positions involved were diametrically opposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you were asked on Thursday, the 7th of April, and it's at page 11.641, about a remark made by Dr. Karadzic that the Serbs had been appointed to be the Muslims' executioners. You remember that remark and no doubt that bit of your evidence, Mr. Trbojevic, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, but it was not said by Dr. Karadzic, it was said by a deputy to the Assembly, Dr. Nedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're quite right, I'm so sorry, Mr. Trbojevic, you're absolutely right about that. And Mr. Tieger asked you at line 6 on page 11.641, "And what do you find to be irresponsible about his remarks?" And Mr. Nedic is mentioned at the foot of the previous page. "What do you find to be irresponsible about his remarks that the Serbs are to be the Muslims' executioners?" And your answer was, "I said that the entire statement was irresponsible and that it represented an outburst, that it did not, in fact, represent anyone's position or anyone's view. He claims here that the Muslims have been planted on us as a nation which is ludicrous. He claims that someone else had envisaged Serbs as executioners of the other nation which once again is completely unfounded." Mr. Trbojevic, you have never heard or read Mr. Krajisnik saying anything remotely like Mr. Nedic's remarks, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you were asked, this is at the next page of that transcript, 11.642, and this time it is Dr. Karadzic, "Dr. Karadzic had stated in the course of an Assembly session, I think it was,, "There is truth in what Mr. Kupresanin has said although known in Europe will say it openly that this conflict was roused in order to eliminate the Muslims," and Mr. Tieger's question to you was. "Did Dr. Karadzic's remarks reflect his understanding of events on the ground as far as you were aware?" Answer: "They most likely did." Mr. Trbojevic, the assertion that the conflict was roused in order to eliminate the Muslims, again, you have never heard or read any such view being expressed by Mr. Krajisnik, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you have no reason to believe Mr. Krajisnik ever has held such a view, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that same day, same transcript, page 11.644, Mr. Tieger put the question to you, "But there was expressed concern, wasn't there, about the number of Muslims who would be in Serb territories because of Muslim birth rates, Muslim demographics." You never heard Mr. Krajisnik express concerns about the birthrate of Muslims, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Going back in that same days's transcript to page 11.629, His Honour Judge Orie asked you a question, he said, line 9, "Did you ever experience in your communications conversations with members of the Presidency that they were unaware of any issue you wanted to raise, you wanted to discuss, or you referred to?" And your answer was, "No." Mr. Trbojevic, you never discussed with Mr. Krajisnik matters of military operation, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, either with him or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You never discussed with Mr. Krajisnik issues relating to prisoner exchange, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You never discussed with Mr. Krajisnik issues concerning detention camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Tieger, is there any need to reexamine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, in your testimony last week on Thursday, I believe, you were asked by Mr. Stewart about Mr. Krajisnik's work with the Assembly and his work on international negotiations and whether or not those constituted full-time jobs. Do you recall that testimony generally, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could focus your attention not on the entire period of time during which you interacted with or worked with Mr. Krajisnik but more narrowly on the period of time from April, May, June, July 1992, do you know offhand how many international negotiations were held during that period of time between members of the Bosnian Serb leadership and international bodies or international negotiators?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I indicated to you that there were, during that period of time, relatively few meetings but that they included two meetings toward the end of April, a meeting in May, and a meeting in mid-July and a meeting in late July, would that be consistent or inconsistent with your recollection, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I further indicated to you that the minutes of those meetings indicate that they were attended by other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership than Mr. Krajisnik, would that be consistent or inconsistent with your knowledge or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a member of the group that was supposed to be involved in those negotiations. I know he travelled abroad to attend those negotiations, but exactly at which meeting he attended, for how long, in which way, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also mentioned his work with the Assembly and, again, I want to focus on the period of April, May, June, and July of 1992. Do you know of any Assembly sessions other than the Assembly session held on May 12th and the Assembly session we looked at the other day, the 17th Assembly session held on July 24 -- 24th to the 26th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know any dates. You have to believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In looking at the minutes of a government session held on May 8th, and if I could have a moment to grab that, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take your time, if not too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that is or will be one of the later tabs, Your Honour, 120, in that vicinity, but I'll indicate that for the registrar on the record at the break, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It reflects a discussion by the members in attendance, and that's the meeting of the National Security Council and the government at that time, to call a session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina as soon as possible. And as we indicated a moment ago, the Assembly session was held on -- the subsequent Assembly session was held on May 12th. Is that generally consistent with your recollection, if you can tell us, of the length of time it takes to organise an Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about this session of the National Defence Council -- National Security Council, rather, because that was the time before I left Sarajevo. The Assembly, the National Assembly was still in Banja Luka and I was still in Sarajevo on the 12th of May, so I don't know how it was organised, that particular meeting of the Assembly, whether helicopters were used or not, because there was no passage from the eastern part of the republic towards Banja Luka by land. How this particular Assembly session was organised, I really don't know. Generally speaking, the convening of an Assembly session involves the collection and copying of material, supplying that material to MPs, organisation of the meetings of deputies' clubs before the meeting and if the Assembly session is taking part in a different location than the usual one, then it also involves finding and organising accommodation, transporting or organising copiers for the background material. So to what extent Krajisnik participated in this, I don't know, but there are quite a lot of activities to organise in connection with an Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, first of all, it's not entirely clear whether this is still in relation to the answers on the full-time job which suggests that there would remain no time to do other things. To be quite honest, this Chamber knows a few people who have three full-time jobs so therefore, we wonder whether it really assists us greatly to talk about full-time jobs not remaining any time left. You are looking at the clock. We would have only very small number of questions. If we would finish the testimony of Mr. Trbojevic during this session and that certainly could not take more than 12 to 13 minutes, at its maximum, 15, we would then be able to prepare for the next witness because we need approximately half an hour to prepare for the protective measures so if we would now have a break, if we would restart at five minutes to 11.00 and then have to break again after 20 minutes, that would perhaps not be a good idea. I don't know how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply inquire. I -- perhaps it's a total misunderstanding on my part, because I -- we -- for various reasons, we didn't get the transcript yesterday in time for me to look at it at all, but I had understood, have I got it completely wrong, I had -- it had been reported to me I had understood that the next witness was not going to give evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there might be some confusion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There clearly is, Your Honour, on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was a bit confused this morning as well. I wondered whether the witness that we -- that testified yesterday would still be on standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you are perfectly right. The thought came up yesterday later, not primarily in my mind, then some preparations were made which means that the witness would be available but of course Ms. Loukas has not been informed about it so I take it that she is not available unless we receive information otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was -- I would rather Your Honour communicated the news to her than I did, but Your Honour, I -- seriously, Your Honour, I do know -- I'm not saying that under no circumstances could the Defence be ready, I'm simply saying that it is expressly understood by Ms. Loukas that this witness wasn't going to be heard today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear and she is perfectly right. At the same time, let's see when we can finish with this witness, otherwise we will be free to do what we want to do the rest of the day and if Ms. Loukas would be available, the witness would at least be available. Mr. Tieger, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had estimated about 15 minutes. I'll do my best to expedite this and make it even faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then perhaps let's not try to rush too much because we have three or four questions from the bench as well. Let's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take the break now until 11.00 so we expect that we would not take more than, at its most, half an hour after the break and perhaps, Mr. Stewart, you could use the break to see whether the -- well-known flexibility of Ms. Loukas would enable her to be here but at the same time, I emphasise quite clearly that she doesn't have to apologise if she's not available because she could not but expect that we would resume with that witness next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very gracious of Your Honour, and in that case, in light of the last remark I will make the call myself rather than delegate it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before the recess [French on the English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [In French] I'm now receiving the French translation on channel 4. Now I can hear it in English. [In English] Yes, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before the recess, I had asked you about the number of times the Assembly met during the period April through July 1992. And is it correct that because the Assembly was not meeting more regularly, that the Presidency and the expanded Presidency took decisions that were then ratified in those Assembly sessions, for example, in the Assembly session we discussed earlier the 17th Assembly session, do you recall that it began with a -- with remarks by Mr. Krajisnik about the long agenda and about the fact that the Presidency had adopted a string of laws and decisions which the Assembly was supposed to ratify, is that consistent with your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that the Presidency adopted and expanded Presidency adopted conclusions and directives which it communicated to the government for the government to implement and I can direct your attention to particular sessions of the government in which that appears to be reflected. For the Court's benefit, I would simply, for examples, tab 23, on June 15th, tab 27 on June 24th, tab 31 on July 11th, but if that's consistent with the witness's recollection, I think there's no need to pull out those individual sessions. Is that consistent with your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that I remember specifically but there is no controversy about that. The Presidency invoked a particular provision from the Constitution, I can't remember exactly now, I think it was Article 80, saying that at the time when the Assembly cannot be convened, the president of the republic has the right to pass a law which is then later verified by the Assembly. That is indeed what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my question after we touched on that subject of the Presidency passing laws later verified by the Assembly, whether the Presidency and expanded Presidency also issued conclusions and directives which were then communicated to the government for implementation. And I cited a number of specific examples, which it's not necessary for you to look at in particular if it's your -- if the fact that the Presidency conveyed such conclusions to the government for implementation is consistent with your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I do not recall specific things. There's no doubt once a law is passed, it is passed, and I have to accept that. As for these other things, I really don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could we cut that short? I think the issue could be approached in a different way. Mr. Trbojevic, did the government ever send back any conclusion, proposal, directive or whatever document from the expanded Presidency for the reason that it was not legally constituted since no state of war had been declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, on Friday, His Honour Judge Hanoteau directed you to some portions of your statement concerning the presence of Main Board members at Assembly sessions and the issue of resulting pressure on the delegates and you also described on that date -- you also described on Friday, events in 1994 at discussions where you indicated there was no chance to even start a discussion in the Assembly about other proposals than what Karadzic and Krajisnik were proposing as a result of members of the party alleging that you or others were traitors. First of all, do you recall, generally, that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the threat of being called a traitor existed in and was raised in the Assembly in 1992 as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly when this was first used but in that kind of situation, when there is a war on several sides, when there are conflicts all over the place, this term "traitor" is very easily defined and very readily used, also easily accepted for officers who, in any way emphasised their affiliation with the former JNA, they would immediately call them traitors, communist officers, all of those who had this nostalgia towards the former Yugoslavia, and the togetherness that prevailed there were called traitors because now a Serbian state was in the making and so on and so forth. So this term traitor was applied very broadly and, as I said later on in the Assembly, too, regarding such big things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I had asked you about the implication of that term and the use of that term in the Assembly in 1992 or earlier, and let me direct your attention, if I may, to a couple of passages from Assembly sessions in that period of time. The first one is the 8th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina of 25 February 1992 which can be found at P64 and P65, tab 93. And I'm quoting here, Mr. Trbojevic, a portion of Mr. Karadzic's remarks found at page 45 of the English. Let's see if it's necessary to distribute it. And that quote is "However, once the party has adopted a policy, anything else is treason. Anything outside the adopted policy is treason. Assisting the enemy cannot be tolerated. Giving him a way out and confusing the people while being a member of that party, of the Assembly, and the party organs, that cannot be. I will not allow it. I will signal to the people: People, this man is a traitor." And if I could also at the same time direct your attention to the second session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on November 21st, 1991, found at P64 and P65, tab 59 at page 12. These are the remarks of Mr. Krajisnik and I quote, "Traitors and outcasts are the most difficult opponents. We would like to send the following message to all those who falter or are neutral, weak, or misguided and who do not feel like traitors. Today, you still have time, tomorrow will be too late." Mr. Trbojevic, is it correct then that the use of and the impression resulting from the term "traitor" also resulted in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit in 1991 and February 1992, this was not of a very serious character yet, it was before the proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and before the Constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and before we left Sarajevo. It was distasteful political vocabulary, if I can put it that way. At least I did not think that this was a serious threat, what we heard just now, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And once the conflict broke out, then the level of the threat or the nature of the threat escalated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when you are in a situation of war, the other side treats you as a member of the hostile forces and then conditionally speaking, your side, if it proclaims you to be a traitor then the situation becomes very serious and you can expect all sorts of things. Criteria are quite different once a war breaks out as compared to a situation when we are still conducting political discussions in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, did the questions in re-examination raise any further need to cross-examine the witness on those portions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's one issue right now for.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's one issue right now, I apologise for being dispute I'm actually distracted by one issue which Mr. Krajisnik is raising which may bear on what Your Honours just asked me. Might I just have a minute, perhaps to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Take your time, and take care that the microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you were asked in fact, by Judge Orie in the course of Mr. Tieger's questions, whether the government had ever returned any document or rejected any document on the basis that the expanded Presidency was not lawfully constituted. You recall that exchange of question and answer five minutes or so ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say whether the government actually received any documentation of any sort purporting to come from the expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that there were laws and some decisions, but specifically what came was something I could not tell the Prosecutor either. I could not give any specific examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it -- is it your position, Mr. Trbojevic, that as far as the technical, legal, and constitutional establishment of an expanded Presidency is concerned, you, yourself, just don't definitively know what the position was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this expanded Presidency had been constituted; however, the basic requirement in the Constitution was to have a state of war declared in order to have this kind of thing operate. I thought that the requirements had not been met for that. Formally, how this was constituted, is something I don't know. I don't know whether there was a special session when this Presidency was promulgated. I think that there was a decision for this Presidency to be expanded, I think. I think I saw it, that it was being expanded in order to include the president of the Assembly and the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trbojevic, you -- you have already said that you didn't attend any meetings of any expanded Presidency or purported expanded Presidency yourself. Is the position that anything you know about whether there were actually meetings of a body called the expanded Presidency comes from what you can see on paper? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that has been gone into in both examination-in-chief and in cross-examination and it's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, under the present circumstances, I will allow Mr. Stewart to put that question. There might be some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, it was envisaged that Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, that is to say, members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were elected at direct elections constitute the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they had the legitimacy of having been elected in direct sections. Afterwards, a three-member Presidency was proclaimed to be the Presidency when that Presidency included Karadzic and when he became the president of that Presidency. So the notion of the Presidency was created once Karadzic came into that body which originally was supposed to be made up of Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic. Now, where does this expanded Presidency come into the picture? I think I saw a decision on the expansion of the Presidency but the notion of the Presidency itself was practically not split up in any way. I do not remember the notion of the Presidency on the one hand and the expanded Presidency on the other hand, as a practical notion, that is, as something that appears in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Tieger, I do not know -- I feel a bit guilty because I said that I'd like to cut matters short when you were referring to tab 23, tab 27, and tab 31. I said perhaps a different approach would cut matters short. If you would like, since I stopped you there and since it seems to have become an issue, if you'd like to further explore that on the basis -- if you feel that there's any need, I would give you an opportunity. I'm not encouraging, but I think it's fair to give you an opportunity to do so because you came with examples and I then put a rather short question to the witness: Did you ever return any proposal, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think that's fine and I think that documentation is available to the Court and largely speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau has a question or perhaps even more for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when Mr. Stewart said "... when a three-member Presidency was proclaimed to be the Presidency," what do you mean when you say "was proclaimed" would you kindly expand on the word "was proclaimed"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remember that Karadzic insisted that he should now be elected to the Presidency and that he should be the president of the Presidency. And I remember that then, by way of comment, we said that that was enough violation of the Constitution and that that certainly could not be in line with the Constitution itself. So this notion of the Presidency and even of the expanded Presidency was first mentioned when Karadzic became part of that Presidency. Now, Krajisnik and Djeric, as people who were supposed to be members of the expanded Presidency, whether they actually became members of that expanded Presidency in real terms, was this an expanded Presidency in a situation of war, whether they did something or were these few papers that came signed by the Presidency come from that three-member Presidency: Karadzic, Plavsic, Koljevic? Believe me, I don't remember the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry, Witness, but you didn't answer my question. I asked you what you meant when you said "a three-member Presidency was proclaimed" to be the Presidency. Now, was it as a result of a law, of a decision? Who made the decision? Was it proclaimed? Was it passed in a local newspaper, in a bulletin, in a gazette, was it stated in an Assembly meeting? I would like to see or find out how it actually happened that this new institution saw the light of day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went through the Assembly, that's for sure. Now, was that yet another addition to that law on the implementation of the Constitution, well, most probably that's the way it was. Most probably it was an amendment to the law on the implementation of the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was that published? Is it something that became official? Did the population, was the population able to know that such an important institutional change had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was. I think it was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I have a second question for you. Concerning your first statement, on page 18 you speak of the work done by the constitutional commission of which you were a member; is that true? You were indeed a member of the constitutional commission. You are speaking of a position adopted by Mr. Krajisnik who wanted to introduce as an official language Serbian and the Cyrillic alphabet as well as the Ekavian dialect. Do you remember that passage of your statement? Please forgive me ignorance but for my information, what were the languages that were being spoken at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, several languages, several dialects, what language could you give me on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those time, the official language was called Serbo-Croatian. Serbo-Croatian. Both scripts were used on an equal footing, the Cyrillic and the Latinic scripts, and they were both taught at school on a regular basis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The dialect was Ijekavian. In practical terms, that means people used localisms such as "lijepo," the word for beautiful. In Serbia they pronounce it as "lepo." In southern parts, it is "lipo" the vowel is "I" rather than "E." This doesn't make it any more difficult to understand each other. In Bosnia, it was "lijepo." In one of the discussions, it was mentioned that we, as Republika Srpska, in our general rapprochement with Serbia should be using the Ekavian dialect in order to be closer to the Serbian version and with other things being as they were, this was met with support; however, it couldn't be enforced because people speak as they speak. For a while, anchors on the radio tried to change the way they speak and it was rather funny sometimes. If you normally speak the Ijekavian dialect and you try to change it overnight, the result can sometimes be ridiculous but at one point, it was a subject of discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said that the idea emanated from Mr. Krajisnik or at least that's how I understood it. Mr. Krajisnik was trying to convict the person called Maksimovic from Foca, [In English] "to convince him that the constitution should stipulate the Serb language, the Cyrillic letter and the Ijekavian dialect."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the question I have is why did he want that? What intention of his did that reflect? What appeared through these discussions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that as a desire to underline one's unity with the people in Serbia proper; however, it simply couldn't go through because it was unnatural, because Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina used the Ijekavian dialect and ultimately it was not adopted in the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then just a point of detail, please forgive me, but you indicated in this same statement that Mr. Krajisnik tried to convince Mr. Maksimovic, and you add, [In English] "Even offered him a gold pen just to comply with his request, but Maksimovic refused simply for the reason that Bosnia and Herzegovina was using this dialect ..." and so on. [Interpretation] What happened, exactly? Why would a gift of a gold pen be convincing in the context of a debate on a linguistic issue, I'd like to understand this a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a discussion between two people who are on good, friendly terms and Krajisnik just said, meaning nothing special, "I'll give you my golden pen, just sign this." I don't even believe it was real gold, for that matter. I believe Krajisnik just said it to underline how much he cared about this thing, how much he wanted the Serb language to become part of that Constitution whereas Maksimovic, who, on the contrary, put great store on the purity of the Bosnian version of the language, was trying to preserve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you, first about the expanded Presidency which was a five-member Presidency, if I well understood.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was published as well, the new expanded Presidency?
